stories.title: Taiwan's chipmakers shine brightest in living memory
stories.summary: Hi everyone from Cheng Ting-Fang, Annie, in Taipei!
stories.title_zh: 台湾芯片制造商迎来有记忆以来最辉煌时刻
stories.content:
Hi everyone from Cheng Ting-Fang, Annie, in Taipei!

This week, I had the chance to meet top executives from two Taiwanese memory chipmakers, Winbond Electronics and Macronix International, at what could be the brightest moment in their companies' histories amid an unprecedented global memory chip shortage. Business has rarely been better, with record earnings being reported, and gross margins of more than 70% for Macronix and Winbond in the July-September quarter.

While memory giants Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Micron, Kioxia, and China's ChangXin Memory Technologies compete fiercely for market share and manufacturing scale in the high-end AI memory sector, Winbond and Macronix have carved out their own niches in customized products and specialized needs. But despite blockbuster results similar to their larger rivals, both companies' share prices have nearly halved from their June peaks amid fears of oversupply and doubts about the AI boom's sustainability.

Macronix founding chairman Miin Wu said the company would offset uncertainty by focusing more on specialized memory chips for industrial, automotive, space and medical applications markets that require lengthy qualification processes and are seeing growing demand. The company also needed to scale back supplies to the gaming console market, with makers such as Nintendo struggling to absorb soaring memory chip prices. Yet even with this sharper focus, Macronix is finding it difficult to keep up with customer demand.

"Every day, customers are chasing us or visiting our company, but our capacity is fully booked, and we can't expand it anytime soon," said Wu, a pioneer of Taiwan's semiconductor industry who founded Macronix in 1989. "Any memory chipmaker that did not shut down over so much market turmoil can enjoy and earn a lot of money now."

Some equipment the company has ordered will not arrive until next year, prompting Wu to take the unusual step of personally joining several meetings with equipment suppliers to push for faster deliveries.

"The equipment vendors think I'm there to yell at them, but instead, I'm there to beg, beg, beg: 'Please, could you shorten the lead times for the machines?'" Wu said.

For Winbond, demand for specialized NOR flash memory, a type of chip used to store code, has been particularly strong. "A single Nvidia Vera Rubin AI data center rack needs some 600 of these chips, compared with just a handful in traditional servers," Winbond President Chen Pei-Ming said.

The company also produces legacy DRAM memory chips and has found that its price quotes are sometimes surprisingly low compared with those of competitors, reflecting how tight the market has become.

However, like Macronix, Winbond faces the major headache of securing production tools and building new facilities fast enough to meet surging demand. Chen said lead times for some equipment, including lithography and metrology tools, now exceed two years. Competing with much larger chipmakers such as TSMC for these machines, Winbond has had to place orders well in advance to ensure timely deliveries.

"Construction of our new plant in Kaohsiung will begin in December," Winbond's Chen said, referring to the southern Taiwanese city. "However, as it is an entirely new facility and cleanroom, we expect only very limited capacity to come online in 2029, with a meaningful production ramp-up not until 2030, so you see how much time is needed to boost capacity now!"

## **Butterfly effects**

China's export controls on tungsten, imposed in early 2025, are sending far-reaching but little-known impacts rippling through the AI chip supply chain. I reported exclusively this week that supplies of tiny microdrills essential for manufacturing printed circuit boards and chip substrates, two of the most sought-after components for building AI infrastructure, are being disrupted.

Needle-like microdrills are made mainly of tungsten carbide, a high-performance material supplied by leading players in Japan, Europe and the U.S. However, these suppliers are vulnerable in their exposure to China's dominance of global tungsten production, which accounts for nearly 80% of the world's output.

The export controls have not only driven prices of tungsten carbide materials outside China up severalfold since last year, but have also fueled the rise of Chinese microdrill makers such as Guangdong Dtech Technology, which reported record earnings and benefits from ready access to a cost-competitive domestic supply chain.

## **Nidec's rise and fall**

Japan's Nidec, renowned for making motors for everything from wind turbines and electric vehicles to robots and machine tools, is embroiled in a corporate governance crisis. Nidec was once one of Japan's most celebrated companies under outspoken founding chairman and CEO Shigenobu Nagamori, who has stepped down amid accounting concerns. The motor maker has been rocked by financial irregularities since last year, raising the risk of a delisting from the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

The Nidec saga underscores the need for a broader overhaul of Japan's corporate culture, where employees often find it difficult to challenge senior executives or speak up against their decisions, Nikkei Asia's **Tsubasa Suruga** and **Mitsuru Obe** report. The crisis also exposes the risks of relying on a single dominant CEO and highlights the need for stronger independent board oversight, more diverse boards and more vocal shareholders across corporate Japan.

Despite governance turmoil, Nidec maintains strong tech advantages in hard disk drive motors, precision machine tools and AI data-center cooling systems.

## **Nvidia's China clampdown**

Chinese tech companies are finding it increasingly difficult to access the powerful Nvidia chips used to train AI.

The U.S. semiconductor giant is ordering its data center partners to reduce their exposure to Chinese customers, the FT's **Zijing Wu, Demetri Sevastopulo** and **Eleanor Olcott** report.

It has told cloud computing clients that they must now sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies, according to five people with knowledge of the matter. There had been no previous restrictions.

Many Chinese groups have relied on overseas leases for advanced AI tasks, including model training. Nvidia's most advanced chips are not allowed to be sold in China due to U.S. export controls.

Nvidia implemented the new requirement over the summer in a pre-emptive effort to reduce the kind of flak it routinely receives from U.S. lawmakers and other critics of its approach to China, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Cloud providers are struggling to comply with the new requirements because it is "difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the U.S.," said one Singapore-based group. "If strictly implemented, it will definitely hurt business."

## **AI debt is ballooning**

Off-balance-sheet debt among U.S. tech giants Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Oracle nearly doubled in just a few months to reach $3.2 trillion by the end of September, according to a Nikkei data analysis by **Kohei Yamada**.

These hidden debts include outstanding purchase commitments, which account for roughly 60% of the total, and leases yet to begin, which make up the remaining 40%. The $3.2 trillion already equals about 80% of the companies' combined assets and could soon exceed them if the current pace continues.

The staggering figures highlight the risks behind the massive AI infrastructure gamble. Investors are increasingly concerned about tech giants' surging investment and concentrated credit risks. If returns fall short of expectations, confidence in these companies could falter, sending shockwaves through the tech sector and broader financial system.

stories.title_zh: Johor 政府、DayOne、PDT 和 Ranhill SAJ 探索向公众供应 excess treated water
stories.content:
Johor is exploring plans to channel excess treated water from DayOne’s water treatment plant to the public, potentially adding to the state’s water supply as water demand rises alongside its economic expansion. The proposal comes as DayOne’s treatment plant processes raw water from Sungai Tebrau, which has a flow of about 80 million liters per day (MLD) while its data center consumes only about 10 MLD, raising the possibility that the excess treated water could be made available to residents.

Chief Minister Datuk Onn Hafiz Ghazi, has yesterday requested DayOne, a Singapore-based hyperscale data center provider, Perbadanan Darul Ta’zim (PDT), a government-linked company, and water operator Ranhill SAJ to hold an urgent technical meeting to assess how the treated water could be distributed for public use.

“… I would like to request that a technical meeting be held as soon as possible to explore and determine how this technology can be utilised to ensure that more treated water can be supplied to the public, in line with Johor’s growing economy,” Onn Hafiz reportedly said as reported by Bernama, Malaysia’s state news agency.

“As for electricity supply, as Jamie (DayOne’s chief executive officer Jamie Khoo) explained earlier, they are working with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) on the use of renewable energy, solar panels and other initiatives to ensure sufficient power for AI (artificial intelligence) operations here.”

According to local reports, Onn Hafiz in his speech at the DayOne Kempas Tech Park Water Treatment Plant Phase Two expansion in Johor, had reportedly said, “DayOne is using polluted water from Sungai Tebrau, treating it and using it for its own operations instead of relying on treated water meant for the public. I have been informed that Sungai Tebrau has a water flow of about 80 million litres per day, while DayOne uses a maximum of about 10 MLD. There is also surplus water from the data centre that could potentially be supplied to the public with an additional treatment process.”

DayOne has invested about RM 25 billion (US$ 6.2 billion) in Johor as of September, with the figure expected to reach RM 28 billion (US$ 6.9 billion) by the end of 2026. The state would continue reviewing data center and AI investments through a technical committee to ensure they serve the interests of Johor and its residents.

stories.title: Green data centre market to hit USD $197.02bn by 2031
stories.summary: Rising demand for AI and cloud services is pushing operators to spend on lower-emission facilities as the market heads towards USD $197.02 billion by 2031.
stories.title_zh: 绿色数据中心市场到2031年将达1970.2亿美元
stories.content:
Fri, 6th Nov 2026 (Today)
The global green data centre market will reach USD $197.02 billion by 2031, up from USD $60.77 billion in 2026, according to MarketsandMarkets.

That would represent a compound annual growth rate of 26.5% as operators and enterprise customers seek lower-emission infrastructure for expanding digital workloads. Demand is being shaped by efforts to cut power use and carbon output while supporting AI, cloud computing and data analytics.

Green data centres are taking a larger role in infrastructure planning as operators pursue more efficient cooling, better energy management and wider use of renewable power. The shift also reflects greater scrutiny of environmental performance and the need for stronger reporting on emissions and energy use.

Cloud and hyperscale facilities are driving much of that change. These sites are under pressure to handle larger computing loads while limiting energy consumption, increasing demand for alternative backup power, efficient equipment and designs that can scale without sharply raising electricity use.

### Market drivers

A key factor in the market's growth is the rise of high-density computing. As AI systems, cloud platforms and large-scale analytics require more processing power, operators are investing in infrastructure designed to reduce waste in power delivery and cooling.

The report also identifies automated monitoring and carbon reporting as a growing part of data centre operations. Operators want clearer visibility over power usage, temperature, airflow and emissions to meet internal sustainability targets and respond to regulatory requirements.

That trend is raising the profile of software tools such as Data Centre Infrastructure Management, or DCIM. The segment is expected to account for a significant share of the market because it combines monitoring of IT and facilities with tools for optimisation, capacity planning and incident management.

DCIM platforms track power usage, voltage, humidity and temperature across facilities. They can also help identify hotspots, detect faults and reduce over-provisioning by improving forecasts for space, cooling and electricity demand.

These systems are also being used to manage asset lifecycles from procurement to retirement. That gives operators more control over utilisation and can reduce unnecessary hardware replacement or duplication across sites.

### Partnership activity

Recent partnerships show where investment is moving. In Europe, Schneider Electric and Vertiv worked with Google and Microsoft on a request for information aimed at finding alternatives to diesel backup generators, reflecting a wider push to cut emissions from resilience systems long reliant on fossil fuels.

Elsewhere, Huawei partnered with Qinghai Big Data Industry Development to develop a data centre in Qinghai's Hainan Prefecture designed to run on 100% clean energy. The project points to growing interest in modular facilities that combine lower-emission electricity sources with large-scale computing needs.

In another example, Schneider Electric partnered with NTT DATA to deploy its EcoStruxure IT DCIM platform across multiple European data centres. The rollout underlines the role software is playing in energy management as operators seek better oversight of facility performance.

### Regional picture

North America currently leads the green data centre market, according to the research, supported by a relatively mature data centre industry, stronger integration of renewable energy and broad enterprise demand for more efficient infrastructure. The region is also facing greater pressure from sustainability rules and corporate decarbonisation targets, shaping purchasing decisions.

That combination has helped shift operators away from older, power-intensive facilities towards designs that place greater emphasis on modularity, efficiency and lower emissions. Industries including hyperscale cloud, financial services, healthcare and AI-led analytics are among those contributing to demand.

Asia Pacific is the fastest-growing regional market. Expansion there is being driven by digitalisation, AI adoption, denser computing deployments and government policies aimed at supporting lower-carbon and net-zero data centre development.

The outlook suggests the next phase of growth will depend on how effectively operators combine scale with lower energy consumption. It also points to vendors offering monitoring, automation, cooling and renewable integration tools remaining closely tied to how the sector adapts to rising computational demand and tighter environmental expectations.

stories.content:
Hong Kong-listed hyperscale data center developer and operator Zhi Sheng Group Holdings Limited today announced that a member of its target acquisition group, Haoyang Data Centre 1 (Thailand) Limited (“HYDC1”), has secured a seven-year US$590 million loan from a Thai bank to fund the construction of its hyperscale AI data center in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor.

HYDC1 occupies a land parcel of approximately 140,302 square metres with first-phase completion targeted within the next six months, paving the way for phased delivery in 2027.

In July 2026, HYDC1 entered into a 10-year data centre colocation services agreement with a leading internet company, representing a contract value of approximately US$1.6 billion (excluding electricity charges). The contract is estimated to account for approximately one-third of the total rental revenue expected upon full completion of the project, said a statement from the firm.

Lai Ningning, CEO and Executive of Zhi Sheng Group, said, “We are honoured to secure this major financing facility and to team up with Mr. Chatchaval as our trusted partner in Thailand. His extensive business acumen and deep local network are invaluable in expanding our business and driving project localisation, enabling us to deliver a world-class AI data centre tailored for the Thai market. As we advance towards first-phase delivery, we remain fully focused on execution to generate sustainable cash flows and long-term value for our partners and shareholders.”

Chatchaval Jiaravanon, a strategic partner of Zhi Sheng Group and Chairman of HYDC1, said, “This milestone financing is a strong testament to our project’s solid fundamentals, rigorous compliance, and execution capability. As we accelerate towards first-phase delivery within six months, this backing reinforces our shared commitment with Zhi Sheng Group to capture Asia’s booming AI computing demand through high-performance data centre infrastructure.”

stories.title: Microsoft to establish second cloud region in Malaysia with Johor Bahru facility
stories.summary: Microsoft will establish its second Malaysian cloud region in Johor Bahru, complementing its existing Kuala Lumpur facility. The expansion targets growing enterprise demand for localized AI and cloud computing infrastructure with data sovereignty compliance.
stories.why_it_matters: Johor Bahru's emergence as a cloud corridor creates a dual-hub strategy for Microsoft in Malaysia, reducing latency for southern ASEAN markets and providing disaster recovery options. Competitors must now evaluate whether single-region deployments in Malaysia remain viable, while Johor's property and power infrastructure will face accelerated demand from both hyperscalers and their supplier ecosystems.

stories.why_zh: Johor Bahru 作为 cloud corridor 的崛起为 Microsoft 在马来西亚创造了双枢纽战略，降低了南部东盟市场的延迟并提供灾难恢复选项。竞争对手现在必须评估在马来西亚的单 region 部署是否仍然可行，而 Johor 的房地产和电力基础设施将面临来自 hyperscalers 及其供应商生态系统的加速需求。
stories.content:
Microsoft plans to establish a second cloud region in Malaysia in Johor Bahru, expanding its presence in the country as demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure grows. The expansion gives businesses more flexibility to scale cloud and AI workloads, manage changing data requirements and respond to regulatory developments while maintaining infrastructure in Malaysia.

The upcoming Southeast Asia 3 (SEA3) region will complement Malaysia West, Microsoft’s first cloud region, which began operations in May 2025 in Greater Kuala Lumpur. Once operational, SEA3 is expected to become Microsoft’s largest cloud region in Southeast Asia. The two regions will allow Malaysian organisations to deploy workloads across separate locations in the country, providing additional options for business continuity, disaster recovery and data management through Microsoft Azure as detailed in a Microsoft Malaysia blog.

“With Malaysia West in Greater Kuala Lumpur and Southeast Asia 3 coming soon in Johor Bahru, Malaysian organizations will have more choice in how they build, run, and scale cloud while advancing their AI innovation,” said Laurence Si, Managing Director, Microsoft Malaysia, during his keynote at Microsoft’s recent Cloud & AI Innovation Day in Kuala Lumpur.

“The organizations that scale AI fastest think platform, not a single datacenter region. A multi-region strategy can strengthen resilience, unlock capacity where and when it is needed, and create room to grow as Malaysia’s AI ambitions evolve. This is how we build Malaysia’s Frontier future together.”

Malaysia West currently operates with three availability zones and offers close to 200 generally available cloud services. Its launch gave organisations access to cloud infrastructure within Malaysia, supporting lower latency and local data residency requirements. SEA3 will feature infrastructure designed to support artificial intelligence workloads. The facility will use closed-loop cooling and air-cooled chillers that eliminate water evaporation during cooling, reducing its reliance on local water resources.

The facility will also use backup generators designed to run on renewable biofuel to reduce net carbon emissions. Microsoft-owned datacenters will be built to achieve at least LEED Gold certification. The addition of SEA3 will give organisations the option of distributing workloads between two Malaysian cloud regions, either operating them simultaneously or maintaining one as a secondary site for recovery.

However, Microsoft noted that multi-region deployments are not necessary for every application, as availability-zone redundancy within a single region may be sufficient for some workloads. Regional deployments are more relevant for mission-critical services and applications requiring additional resilience or serving users across different locations.

stories.title: Water Usage Effectiveness and AI: How cooling choices shape data center water use
stories.summary: What WUE measures, how cooling technologies balance water and energy use, and what customers should consider when comparing data centers. The post Water Usage Effectiveness and AI: How Cooling Choices Shape Data Center Water Use appeared first on Digital Edge DC .
stories.title_zh: 用水效率与AI：冷却选择如何塑造数据中心用水
stories.content:
The growth of AI and other high-density workloads is putting greater focus on how data centers manage energy, water and cooling. Water and energy performance increasingly influence data center selection and sustainability reporting. Cooling designs play a central role in moving heat out of the building, and that requires a balance between electricity and water use. That balance shapes a facility’s PUE and WUE figures. This article covers what those metrics measure, how each cooling technology affects them, and how to compare data centers in context.

## What is water usage effectiveness?

Water usage effectiveness, or WUE, expresses how much water a facility uses for every unit of energy delivered to IT equipment. It is written in liters per kilowatt-hour, so a WUE of 1.35 means roughly 1.35 liters of water consumed for each kilowatt-hour of IT load. A lower WUE indicates less on-site water consumption per unit of IT energy, although the cooling design and water source remain important context.

The metric covers water consumed on site, which in practice means water lost to evaporation in cooling towers or evaporative systems, plus smaller volumes used for humidity control and water treatment. It is measured over a year rather than at a moment, because evaporation varies enormously with weather. As with PUE, the figure describes a facility’s design and operating choices rather than its absolute environmental impact, so the source of the water matters alongside the volume.

## How is WUE different from PUE?

PUE measures energy overhead: total facility energy divided by IT energy. WUE measures water consumption against the same IT energy base. They share a denominator, which is what makes them comparable, and they often move in opposite directions.

Evaporative heat rejection can reduce mechanical refrigeration and improve PUE while increasing water consumption. Mechanical cooling with a closed water loop may use less water but require more energy. The appropriate balance depends on climate, electricity supply and local water availability. PUE and WUE are therefore most useful when reviewed together with the underlying cooling design. PUE remains the more widely published of the two, partly because it applies to every facility while WUE applies only to water-cooled sites. Our article on questions ESG leaders should ask covers the wider set of metrics worth requesting.

## How do cooling technologies balance water and energy use?

Heat rejection methods sit on a spectrum from no water to high water consumption. Working from the dry end:

- **Air-cooled chillers and direct expansion systems** reject heat to the air through refrigerant and fans, consuming essentially no water. Their energy needs may increase, particularly in hot climates, so PUE rises as ambient temperature does.
- **Closed-loop and hybrid cooling towers** circulate water that is cooled without being evaporated, or evaporate only during hot periods. Water use is modest, balancing predictable water use with energy performance.
- **Open cooling towers** evaporate water continuously to reject heat. This is energy-efficient and widely used, and it is the main source of water consumption in conventional data center designs.
- **Adiabatic and evaporative systems** pre-cool incoming air by evaporating water, lowering energy use substantially in dry climates and much less so in humid ones.

Air-side economization, often called free cooling, cuts across this spectrum. Where the outside air is cool enough for enough of the year, it reduces both energy and water use, which is why cooler markets have an inherent advantage. In Digital Edge’s South Korea portfolio, the SEL5 development in Ansan pairs a chiller plant with integrated free cooling, targeting an annualized PUE below 1.25.

## How can cooling design respond to local climate?

Cooling performance depends on matching heat-rejection technology to local temperature and humidity. NARRA1 in Manila, the Philippines lists a designed annual PUE of 1.24, a designed peak PUE of 1.35, and a designed WUE of 1.082; EDGE2 in Jakarta, Indonesia lists a designed annual PUE of 1.25 and the same designed WUE. For context, the Uptime Institute’s global survey has placed the industry average PUE at around 1.55. Manila and Jakarta are both close to the hardest case for evaporative cooling, since humid air absorbs less additional moisture, which is what makes these design figures worth noting. Our Philippines data centers and Indonesia data centers pages cover both facilities in more detail.

## Does liquid cooling use more or less water?

Liquid cooling does not determine water consumption by itself. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling and immersion cooling move heat away from the processor more efficiently than air does, but they do not determine how that heat leaves the building. A liquid-cooled hall can reject heat through a dry cooler, a closed loop, or an evaporative tower, and the water consumption follows that choice rather than the liquid loop itself.

This distinction is important for high-density and AI-ready environments. What liquid cooling does change is the temperature at which heat is available. Because it captures heat in a warmer, more concentrated form than air cooling, it widens the range of conditions in which heat can be rejected without mechanical refrigeration, which tends to help both figures. The CGK Campus in Indonesia is designed with direct-to-chip liquid cooling and recycled water systems, targeting an annualized PUE of 1.25. In Thailand, the BKK Campus uses hybrid closed-loop cooling towers specifically to reduce water consumption. Both are liquid-capable designs that handle heat rejection differently, which is the point.

## Why does a WUE figure need its boundary stated?

Because the same number can describe very different situations, and the qualifiers carry most of the meaning. Three of them matter most.

The first is scope. WUE applies only to facilities that use water-based cooling, so an air-cooled site is not comparable and is normally excluded rather than reported as zero.

The second is whether the figure is a design target or a measured result. Digital Edge’s facility specifications label theirs explicitly as designed PUE and designed WUE, which is the distinction worth looking for: a design figure describes what the engineering is built to achieve under defined conditions, while an operating figure describes what a year of real weather and real load produced.

The third is the water source. A facility consuming recycled or non-potable water places very different pressure on local supply than one drawing the same volume from municipal drinking water. At the Navi Mumbai campus, liquid cooling is supported by 10 million liters per day of recycled greywater, with a target WUE below 1.75.

## How should WUE be assessed for AI and high-density workloads?

AI and other high-density workloads increase the importance of understanding both facility efficiency and total resource use. Consistent reporting boundaries help customers compare different facilities and cooling designs.

The main distinction is between on-site and off-site water. WUE, as described above, counts water consumed at the facility. It does not count water used to generate the electricity the facility draws, which can be significant on grids where thermoelectric generation dominates, since those plants consume water for their own cooling. Some analyses report that second figure, often called source water, alongside or instead of site water. Stating the boundary clearly helps ensure meaningful comparisons.

Scale is the other factor. AI workloads raise power density, so a hall running AI equipment draws more energy and, depending on how heat is rejected, can consume more water in absolute terms even where the ratios stay flat or improve. Because efficiency metrics are ratios, they should be reviewed alongside total consumption and IT load. Location also matters: climate, water availability and electricity supply influence the most appropriate cooling strategy for each facility.

Together, these measures help customers understand how a facility manages water and energy under its specific operating conditions.

## Conclusion

WUE is most useful when considered alongside PUE, cooling design, climate and water source. The appropriate balance between water and energy use varies by location and operating requirement.

For teams evaluating facilities or gathering figures for their own reporting, they should ask four questions: which heat rejection method the site uses, whether the figures are designed or measured, what the reporting excludes, and where the water comes from. These questions enable more informed and consistent comparisons.

## Talk to Digital Edge

Digital Edge publishes efficiency and water metrics across its platform in our ESG reporting, covering facilities from Manila to Incheon — talk to our team about the cooling design and reported figures at any site in our colocation portfolio.

stories.title: ING said to be seller of US$500 mil data centre loan portfolio
stories.summary: (Nov 6): Dutch bank ING is putting up for sale a roughly US$500 million portfolio of data centre loans all at once, according to people familiar with the matter. The rare auction comes just days after a Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections raised doubts about the future of many of the projects.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: ING据称正在出售5亿美元data centre贷款组合
stories.content:
The bank is taking offers for a dozen loans via a so-called bids-wanted-in-competition process, the people added, asking not to be identified because the information is private. The loans for sale include a US$25 million slice backing a massive data centre site that’s part of OpenAI, SoftBank Group Corp and Oracle Corp’s joint Stargate project in New Mexico. It’s the location where Oracle sent the developer a notice citing force majeure.

A representative for ING declined to comment.

It is also looking to offload debt tied to operators such as Vantage Data Centers and CyrusOne, said the people. Bids on the loans are due Nov 19 and must be at least US$10 million in size, they added.

The auction, among the first of its kind that exclusively contains data centre debt, underscores the market pessimism that has erupted over the AI buildout in the wake of the US elections. In Texas, where many developers have a presence, the Democratic governor-elect has called for an immediate moratorium on construction for the projects.

The Nasdaq 100 closed 6.4% lower Thursday, wiping out US$2.3 trillion in value and extending weeks of concerns from Wall Street investors who have been retreating from the AI trade. In the high-yield market, junk bonds tied to data centre developers or projects, including CoreWeave Inc and Galaxy Digital Inc, saw some of the biggest declines.

Wall Street is broadly contending with the risk that the credit market is nearing the limit for how much AI debt it can absorb amid questions of whether revenue can justify the breathtaking spending.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Apollo Global Management Inc are looking to syndicate portions of the largest chip financing on record tied to SpaceX, *Bloomberg* reported this week. They committed to the deal in October before pricing it, and now face the prospect of the market turning against them.

stories.title: Turner & Townsend names Niralee Shah Asia Pacific lead
stories.summary: The hire comes as demand for digital infrastructure surges across Asia Pacific, with clients seeking help on complex data centre builds and energy issues.
stories.title_zh: Turner & Townsend任命Niralee Shah为亚太区负责人
stories.content:
Fri, 6th Nov 2026 (Today)
Turner & Townsend has appointed Niralee Shah as Data Centre Services Lead for Asia Pacific, based in Singapore.

She will support the growth and delivery of the company's data centre business across the region, working with clients and regional leaders on service delivery, client relationships and programmes in key markets.

The appointment comes as investment in data centres across Asia Pacific continues to rise, driven by demand for cloud services, artificial intelligence and broader digital transformation. Turner & Townsend has more than 1,000 specialists supporting hyperscale and colocation clients across 14 markets in the region.

### Regional demand

Asia Pacific has become a major market for data centre development as operators and investors expand capacity to meet rising computing and storage needs. Advisory and programme management firms have also been adding sector specialists as clients seek support on complex builds, supply chains and energy-related issues.

Turner & Townsend is a programme management company with more than 23,000 people in 64 countries, working across real estate, infrastructure, energy and natural resources. The business is majority-owned by CBRE Group, while its partners retain a significant non-controlling interest.

Shah brings more than 15 years of experience in business operations, strategic planning, financial management and client services across Asia Pacific. Her background includes roles with organisations in real estate, technology and professional services, tied to business growth, operations and large infrastructure programmes.

She has worked across markets and cultures in the region and is fluent in English, Japanese and Hindi. Her remit will span Asia Pacific as Turner & Townsend looks to deepen its position in the data centre segment.

Commenting on the appointment, Sumit Mukherjee outlined the company's view of regional market conditions.

"Asia Pacific remains one of the world's most dynamic regions for data centre development, with unprecedented demand for digital infrastructure creating significant opportunities across its markets.

"Niralee's appointment further strengthens our regional team and reinforces our commitment to helping clients successfully deliver critical digital infrastructure programmes, combining our market-leading expertise in data centre delivery, power, transmission and renewables," said Sumit Mukherjee, Managing Director, Head of Real Estate, Asia Pacific, Turner & Townsend.

### Growth focus

The hire reflects continued competition among professional services firms to secure work tied to digital infrastructure expansion in Asia Pacific. Data centre projects in the region have drawn interest from property groups, cloud providers, private capital and engineering firms, particularly in markets where demand for capacity is outstripping supply.

Singapore remains a key base for many regional executives in the sector, even as development activity spreads across North Asia, South-East Asia and other fast-growing markets. Companies operating in the space are also dealing with land constraints, grid access, sustainability requirements and construction costs.

Shah said the market backdrop made the move significant for both the company and its clients.

"I'm excited to join Turner & Townsend at a defining moment for the data centre sector. Demand across Asia Pacific is being reshaped by AI, cloud and digital transformation, and clients need partners who can navigate that complexity with confidence. Turner & Townsend has an exceptional platform of expertise and experience, and I see significant opportunity to build on that foundation. I look forward to working with our clients and teams across Asia Pacific to support their ambitions and contribute to the continued growth of the business," said Shah.

stories.title: VAST Data says 14 customers committed USD $10 billion
stories.summary: Four customers each committed more than USD $1 billion as demand for AI storage systems pushed VAST's aggregate customer pledges above USD $10 billion.
stories.title_zh: VAST Data称14家客户承诺投入100亿美元
stories.content:
Fri, 6th Nov 2026 (Today)
VAST Data says 14 of its customers have made aggregate commitments of more than USD $10 billion for its software and related hardware. Four of those customers each committed more than USD $1 billion.

The commitments were made in the first three quarters of VAST's current fiscal year by a small subset of the more than 1,000 organisations it serves. Each of the 14 customers committed more than USD $100 million to VAST Data-based system buildouts.

The disclosure provides a measure of spending now flowing into data infrastructure for artificial intelligence training and inference. It also offers fresh detail on customer concentration at a company valued at USD $30 billion after a Series F funding round earlier this year that included NVIDIA.

VAST sells software for large-scale data environments, with platform hardware included in customer deployments. Its systems now support nine of the top 10 frontier AI labs, according to the company.

### Supply planning

VAST also said it had structured agreements with supply chain partners to align more than 200 exabytes of flash capacity through 2029. The arrangements are intended to match expected demand from its largest customers and help users plan infrastructure purchases amid pressure on NAND flash supply.

NAND flash is a core component in enterprise storage systems used in data centres. Bringing new supply to market can take years because of the investment required in fabrication plants, making long-range planning important for suppliers and buyers when demand rises sharply.

According to VAST, the data capacity being delivered by its partners now represents a significant share of global NAND flash output for enterprise data centres. It did not disclose the financial terms of the supply agreements or identify the manufacturers involved.

Renen Hallak, founder and chief executive officer of VAST Data, linked the spending to broader changes in how AI infrastructure is being built. "Growth at this scale only happens when an entire industry is rebuilding at once. That's what the new AI stack is. It's being built for models and agents, not people and applications, and data sits at the centre of it. The companies building it at the largest scale, for people, agents and now robots, are choosing VAST to anchor it," Hallak said.

The latest figures come as investors and technology groups continue to channel large sums into AI-related computing, networking and storage. While graphics processing units have drawn much of the attention, storage and data systems are also seeing strong demand as companies assemble the infrastructure needed to train models, run inference workloads and manage growing volumes of data.

That has increased pressure across the semiconductor supply chain. Flash storage is widely used in data-intensive environments because operators need fast access to large datasets, and supply constraints can have knock-on effects on deployment timetables for cloud providers, AI labs, enterprises and public sector users.

Jeff Denworth, co-founder of VAST Data, said the company's supply planning was tied to customer requirements. "Planning for hundreds of exabytes isn't only about protecting our customers' growth projections. It's about keeping flash available to hundreds of clouds, so that every AI builder, not just the largest, has the capacity it needs to build and compete," Denworth said.

VAST did not name the 14 customers behind the commitments or break out how much of the aggregate total related to software versus hardware. It also did not say how much of the committed spending had already been converted into recognised revenue.

Even so, the figures point to a small number of buyers placing very large bets on storage and data architecture as AI infrastructure scales up. The largest disclosed group alone accounts for more than USD $10 billion in planned spending tied to VAST systems.

stories.title: US data-centre backlash may lower odds of AI investment bust
stories.summary: (Nov 5): The backlash against data centers evident in this week's US midterm elections raises new risks for a key source of economic growth. But restrictions on development could ultimately reduce the odds of a downturn by keeping the AI investment boom in check. Around half of planned ...

stories.title_zh: 美国data centre反弹可能降低AI投资泡沫破裂的几率
stories.content:
(Nov 5): The backlash against data centers evident in this week's US midterm elections raises new risks for a key source of economic growth. But restrictions on development could ultimately reduce the odds of a downturn by keeping the AI investment boom in check.

Around half of planned expansion nationwide is vulnerable to increased scrutiny and pushback from Democrats who clinched historic victories in states like Texas, Georgia and Ohio. Many of the candidates campaigned against unfettered data-center construction and will likely seek to quickly deliver on what has become a wildly popular position across the country this year.

The new mandate is arriving just as technology investment has become more important for the economy than ever before. But the scale and speed of the boom have also inevitably raised concerns about an eventual bust.

"If some of these moratoriums or regulatory pressures slow some of this buildout, it almost prevents you from blowing too big of a bubble," said Brett Ryan, an economist at Deutsche Bank Securities. "This is like a good excuse to kill some projects here that were already looking shaky."

The paradox illustrates a central tension in the US economy of the post-pandemic era: Growth has become unusually reliant on a handful of sectors pouring enormous sums into a new technology with a payoff that's so far been difficult to quantify.

Thursday's selloff in AI-linked stocks also offered a reminder that the boom has helped support consumer spending through rising household wealth, a channel that could work in reverse if the trade unwinds quickly.

Over the last year, capital expenditures on information processing equipment and software alone have given the US economy the biggest boost on record, eclipsing even their contribution at the peak of the 1990s dot-com boom.

A report Thursday also showed broader economic growth is being propelled almost entirely by productivity enhancements, though economists said the prospective boost from AI is largely yet to appear in the numbers.

Monthly construction spending on data centers, meanwhile, has almost doubled over the last 12 months, to nearly $100 billion on an annualized basis.

For now, economists don't foresee an immediate pullback because much of the capacity that will come online next year is already under construction. This week's election results, however, could have a bigger impact on the outlook for 2028 to the extent that groundbreaking on new facilities begins to slow.

Ryan said Deutsche Bank had already been projecting slower growth in investment by then. Following Tuesday's elections, "my knee-jerk reaction would be, OK, I don't have to raise my 2028 forecast anytime soon," he said.

The impact will depend on the specific shape any new restrictions might take. About 45% of planned data-center capacity is in states where newly elected Democrats campaigned on such limits, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

Texas alone accounts for 25% of the total, and Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to be elected governor there since 1990, has vowed to halt new approvals. Georgia and Ohio are also getting Democratic governors for the first time in decades. In the former, Keisha Lance Bottoms campaigned on a statewide pause, while in the latter Amy Acton has proposed stricter conditions on new projects.

States with restrictions in place prior to the midterms have so far opted for temporary measures rather than permanent bans. In July, New York became the first to announce a pause on new environmental permits for hyperscale data center construction for up to one year.

Many smaller localities, however, have gone further. Monterey Park, California; Harford County, Maryland; and East Rutherford, New Jersey have all imposed some form of outright prohibition on data centers this year, and several Ohio municipalities this week voted to adopt similar measures.

Sarah Bianchi, a strategist at Evercore ISI, said she expects state moratoriums would last no more than a year as policymakers decide what restrictions to put in place, including whether to grandfather existing projects or impose rules based on project size.

Given the breadth of the backlash, though, "It's not like it's going to be super easy to go somewhere else in this environment," she said.

stories.title: NVIDIA launches Minerva to spot AI factory faults early
stories.summary: The software aims to cut downtime and boost output for operators of massive GPU clusters by turning event storms into likely root causes.
stories.title_zh: NVIDIA推出Minerva以早期发现AI factory故障
stories.content:
NVIDIA has launched Minerva, an AIOps platform for AI factory operations designed to help teams spot faults earlier and maintain output across large AI infrastructure estates.

Minerva brings together telemetry from infrastructure and AI workloads, including GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers, and the jobs running across them. The platform uses AI models to analyse operational data and turn it into alerts, incident groupings, and remediation suggestions.

The release reflects the growing operational challenge facing operators of large AI clusters, where a single underperforming component can affect a wider training or inference workload. AI factories can involve hundreds of thousands of GPUs connected across high-speed networks, making it difficult for operations, networking, reliability, and machine learning teams to work from a single view of events.

### Single view

According to NVIDIA, Minerva creates a dynamic knowledge graph that maps physical infrastructure, such as GPUs, SuperNICs, switches, and cables, alongside the jobs using those resources. The model is intended to help operators trace a slowdown in a training run or service back to the infrastructure affecting it.

The system analyses billions of data points an hour using supervised and unsupervised machine learning. It is designed to learn what normal behaviour looks like, identify anomalies, predict failures, and correlate related events based on a site's topology.

Rather than presenting operations teams with large volumes of separate alerts, Minerva groups related signals into a smaller number of incidents with a likely root cause. It also includes a native AI assistant and can connect to external agentic AI tools, giving staff a natural-language interface to query cluster health and review proposed actions.

Teams can either keep human operators responsible for implementing fixes or connect the platform to automation through infrastructure application programming interfaces and external systems.

### Yield focus

The platform is centred on what NVIDIA calls AI factory yield, which it defines through measures such as GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime, and token production. The aim is to help operators extend the time between interruptions, shorten repair times, and reduce the volume of low-value alerts that can obscure more serious issues.

These features target a key commercial issue for companies building AI data centres: keeping expensive computing assets running at useful output for as long as possible. In large training environments, symptoms such as a hotter-than-normal GPU or a storage drive losing performance under load may seem minor in isolation, but can still affect a much larger job.

According to NVIDIA, IREN is already using the software, while Aolani, Bitdeer AI, IBM, Jio, Lambda, Quake AI, and Tesla plan to deploy it. Dell Technologies, Lenovo, and Supermicro will also offer Minerva within their AI factory operations portfolios.

IREN provided a customer example. "As we scale our AI factories, the key to providing the best service for our customers is maximizing the productivity of our GPUs," said Denis Skrinnikoff, Chief Technology Officer at IREN. "NVIDIA Minerva gives our operations team one view across the network, the GPUs and the jobs running on them, so we focus more on proactive maintenance rather than troubleshooting. That visibility strengthens our operating model for the infrastructure we're building next."

The launch adds to a broader push by infrastructure suppliers to move beyond selling chips and servers into the software used to run AI estates day to day. Operators are increasingly looking for tools that combine hardware telemetry with workload data, particularly as AI systems grow in size and as downtime or degraded performance becomes more costly.

For NVIDIA, Minerva also extends its reach deeper into the operational layer of AI data centres by linking its GPUs and networking products with software that monitors how those systems behave in production. The platform is intended to turn event storms into a focused incident with a probable root cause.

stories.title: Rakon launches timing portfolio for AI data centres
stories.summary: Better timing is becoming a bottleneck in AI clusters, prompting Rakon to add clocks and oscillators for networking, synchronisation and compute layers.
stories.title_zh: Rakon推出面向AI data centre的timing产品组合
stories.content:
Fri, 6th Nov 2026 (Today)
Rakon has launched a timing portfolio for AI data centres and hyperscale infrastructure, covering the communication, synchronisation and compute layers in AI systems.

The portfolio includes oven-controlled crystal oscillators, temperature-compensated crystal oscillators and crystal oscillators for optical transceivers, switching equipment, network timing and compute hardware. The products are aimed at applications ranging from high-speed data centre networking to network interface cards, data processing units and AI accelerators.

The move reflects growing attention on parts of AI infrastructure beyond the processors themselves. As operators build larger clusters of interconnected GPUs and other accelerators, timing accuracy is becoming more important to keep data moving across optical links and distributed compute resources aligned.

In communications, Rakon is targeting reference clocks used in optical transceivers, SERDES and networking equipment. These systems handle large volumes of traffic between AI accelerators, where signal quality and timing stability can affect efficiency across a cluster.

For synchronisation, the range is designed to operate across network layers, from grandmaster clocks and switching infrastructure to network interface cards and processors. This part of the portfolio includes digitally controlled OCXOs, IC-OCXO devices and long-holdover discrete OCXOs.

At the compute level, Rakon is extending timing products into the tray itself, where they can be used in NICs, DPUs and AI accelerators. The line-up includes digitally controlled OCXOs and TCXOs, along with its Niku Ultra Stable TCXOs and compact high-stability TCXOs.

Wil Hsieh, Head of Products (Commercial BU) at Rakon, linked the launch to the wider build-out of AI systems.

"AI performance isn't determined by processing power alone," Hsieh said.

"Keeping data moving quickly and compute resources working efficiently also depends on the timing infrastructure around them. Better timing helps reduce communication and synchronisation bottlenecks, enabling AI infrastructure to make more effective use of its available compute performance. Rakon's portfolio addresses that challenge from optical connectivity and network synchronisation right through to the compute tray."

### New products

A central addition to the range is the Vulcan ROV7050XD digitally controlled OCXO, which is now sampling. Intended for network timing and synchronisation in AI infrastructure, it combines digital control with programmable frequencies in a 7 x 5 mm-class hermetic package.

Rakon said the ROV7050XD supports frequencies up to 1 GHz, with frequency stability of ±10 ppb and a frequency slope of ±0.5 ppb/°C. The device uses I2C for frequency tuning, allowing designers to adjust output frequency requirements without changing hardware.

The product sits in a part of the market where network timing must balance precision, size and flexibility. In large AI deployments, synchronisation devices are used across scale-up and scale-out architectures, including spine, leaf and Top-of-Rack switching.

Rakon is also extending its XO line to higher frequencies with a new high-frequency, ultra-low-jitter differential series. The current RXO2520NT and RXO2016NT models operate at 500 MHz, and the series is intended to reach 1.25 GHz.

According to Rakon, the existing models deliver 30 fs RMS phase jitter and ±10 ppm FvT. They are available in 2.5 x 2.0 mm and 2.0 x 1.6 mm footprints, with smaller package sizes under development.

### AI timing

The launch highlights a less visible part of the AI supply chain. While much of the investment focus has fallen on GPUs, networking silicon and memory, timing components support communication between systems and co-ordination across racks.

As data rates rise, reference clocks are being pushed to higher frequencies, particularly in optical interconnects and next-generation networking equipment. At the same time, tighter synchronisation is becoming more important as AI workloads are distributed across larger numbers of processors.

Rakon said its development work in digital control, high-frequency differential technology, XMEMS resonator technology and ASIC design is feeding into the new line-up. Those technologies are being used to produce smaller devices with higher frequencies, greater stability and lower jitter for data centre applications.

Hsieh said AI infrastructure is changing quickly.

"AI infrastructure is evolving extremely quickly, particularly around network speed and synchronisation," he said.

"Our Vulcan ASIC platform with Digital Control brings greater flexibility to precision network timing, while our new high-frequency XO platform combines ultra-low jitter with increasingly higher frequencies and smaller form factors. These developments are about helping customers get more performance from the infrastructure connecting their AI compute resources."

stories.title: Crusoe unveils 3.5 MW modular data centre for Nvidia AI racks
stories.summary: Crusoe has launched its sixth-generation modular data centre platform, Spark Liquid, designed for Nvidia GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks. The unit supports up to 3.5 MW of compute capacity and features direct liquid cooling.
stories.title_zh: Crusoe 发布 3.5 MW 模块化数据中心，支持 Nvidia AI racks
stories.content:
Crusoe has introduced its sixth-generation modular data centre platform, Spark Liquid, designed to support up to 3.5 MW of compute capacity.The new unit is built for Nvidia GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks. Crusoe stated that Spark Liquid delivers five times the compute density of earlier Spark generations.Production for Spark Liquid will begin in Brighton, Colorado, in 2027, joining the company’s existing Spark line. The Spark platform will also support Nvidia’s recently announced DSX POD blueprint for modular infrastructure.
### Modular approach for AI infrastructure

Modular data centres are gaining traction for AI infrastructure due to constraints in power, predictability, and time to deployment, according to Bryan Schramm, head of Spark at Crusoe. Factory-built units can utilise available power in smaller blocks, shortening grid interconnect timelines.Building in a factory enhances delivery date reliability, which is crucial for organisations reserving capacity in advance. This approach also shortens time to revenue for operators by bringing capacity online quicker.Spark Liquid is designed around a closed-loop direct liquid cooling (DLC) system for rack-scale systems like Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72. DLC efficiently removes heat at high power densities, necessary for the Spark Liquid’s design.The water recirculates in a closed loop, needing minimal ongoing water and avoiding evaporative loss. Efficiency will vary with climate, with each deployment designed for local conditions.Each Spark Liquid unit is built in Crusoe’s factory and shipped ready to deploy in clusters. Crusoe acquired electrical manufacturer Easter-Owens Electric in 2022 to bring manufacturing in-house.Bryan Schramm noted that moving variability into a controlled factory environment helps Crusoe adopt and deploy next-generation GPUs faster. Nvidia’s standardisation on modular designs reinforces Crusoe’s long-standing approach.

Infineon Technologies AG and Wolfspeed Inc. have entered a new multi-year supply agreement for 200-millimeter silicon carbide (SiC) wafers, shifting Infineon's existing supply relationship from 150-millimeter to 200-millimeter substrate technology.SiC semiconductors are essential for electrification and energy efficiency applications driving global decarbonisation, including electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, and AI datacenter power infrastructure.The agreement directly supports Infineon's conversion to 200-millimeter SiC manufacturing. stories.title: Two dead and five injured following fire at Panasonic chip packaging facility in Taiwan
stories.summary: Two people have died and five people were injured following a fire and explosion at a Taiwanese factory owned by Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials.
stories.title_zh: Panasonic台湾芯片封装设施火灾致两人死亡五人受伤
stories.content:
Two people have died and five people were injured following a fire and explosion at a Taiwanese factory owned by Panasonic Industrial Devices Materials.

According to a report from Focus Taiwan, the fire broke out at the five-story factory in Hsinchu at around 2:00 am local time on November 4. More than 20 members of staff were believed to be working on the production lines when the incident occurred.

The report added that 12 vehicles and 23 firefighters were dispatched to the site, and heavy machinery was required to dig through the debris. It was then that the deceased workers, who had previously been reported missing, were discovered.

The five injured workers were transported to hospital. No information about their condition has been publicly disclosed.

Initial reports suggested the fire was caused by flammable chemical solvents, such as methanol and methyl ethyl ketone, which are used at the factory. However, in a statement, the Hsinchu Fire Bureau said that the exact cause of the incident was still under investigation. The bureau additionally noted that the factory had passed a fire safety inspection in August.

*DCD* has contacted Panasonic for comment.

First opened in December 1987, the Hsinchu factory is used by Panasonic to manufacture printed circuit boards and semiconductor packaging materials. A semiconductor materials R&D center was established on the site in April 2019.

*DCD's sympathies go out to the family and friends of the victims.*

stories.title: ABB teams up with Korean shipbuilder Hanwha on power and control systems for offshore data centers
stories.summary: South Korean shipbuilding company Hanwha Ocean has inked a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with ABB to develop advanced power and control systems for floating data centers.
stories.title_zh: ABB与韩国造船商Hanwha合作开发海上数据中心的power和control systems
stories.content:
South Korean shipbuilding company Hanwha Ocean has inked a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with ABB to develop advanced power and control systems for floating data centers.

According to the companies, the MoU aims to improve the technical capabilities of floating data centers by combining Hanwha’s experience in offshore design and construction with ABB’s expertise in data center power solutions.

Earlier this year, Hanwha showcased a self-developed 60MW-class floating data center. The concept envisions developing data center capacity on a floating structure that can generate power offshore and use seawater for cooling.

Under the terms of the MoU with ABB, the companies said they will work together through May next year on power system design reviews and the development of operating and control technologies, targeting stable power supply and efficient operation of floating data centers.

Hanwha will lead the basic design and power system configuration of the floating data center and set design standards for power generation equipment, which are expected to be based on liquefied natural gas (LNG) engines. ABB, in turn, will analyze the reliability and power quality of the electrical system based on the design provided and subsequently conduct a range of technical reviews in order to improve the operating efficiency of the power systems.

"As the AI industry grows, technologies that support stable power supply and efficient operation of data centers are becoming more important," said Heo Yoon, executive vice president and head of Hanwha Ocean's Product Strategy and Technology Institute. "Through this partnership with ABB, we will raise the technical maturity of floating data center solutions suited to marine environments and broaden the foundation for growth in our future offshore business."

There has been a rising tide of offshore and floating data center concepts in recent years. Keppel has started work on a 25MW floating facility in Singapore, due to come online in 2028, while US-based Panthalassa wants to harness the power of waves for floating data centers at sea.

Floating wind firm Aikido has also announced its entrance into the data center space with the launch of a floating offshore wind platform integrated with a modular AI-focused data center.

Other companies working on floating projects include Seatrium, Mocean, and Atomarine. *DCD* took an in-depth look at the emerging compute-at-sea sector in issue 52 of the magazine.

stories.title: APAC operator PDG secures $1.3 billion for Malaysia build-out
stories.summary: Princeton Digital Group has raised $1.3 billion in financing to accelerate its data center build-out across Malaysia. The funding supports the Singapore-headquartered operator's expansion in one of APAC's fastest-growing digital infrastructure markets.
stories.why_it_matters: PDG's substantial capital raise validates Malaysia as a primary destination for data center investment capital, competing directly with Singapore's historical dominance in the region. The funding volume suggests institutional investors are comfortable with Malaysia's regulatory trajectory and power infrastructure commitments, though multiple simultaneous large-scale projects may strain construction labor markets and grid interconnection queues.
stories.title_zh: APAC运营商PDG获得13亿美元用于Malaysia建设
stories.summary_zh: Princeton Digital Group 已筹集 13 亿美元融资，以加速其在马来西亚的 data center 建设。该资金支持这家总部位于新加坡的运营商在 APAC 增长最快的数字基础设施市场之一的扩张。
stories.why_zh: PDG 的大量资本筹集验证了马来西亚作为 data center 投资资本主要目的地的地位，直接与新加坡在该地区的历史主导地位竞争。该资金规模表明机构投资者对马来西亚的监管轨迹和电力基础设施承诺感到满意，尽管多个同时进行的 large-scale 项目可能给建筑劳动力市场和电网互联队列带来压力。
stories.content:
APAC data center firm Princeton Digital Group (PDG) has secured more than $1 billion in new financing to fund its build-out in Malaysia.

The company this week announced that it has secured approximately $1.3 billion (\~RM 5.1 billion) in green financing for its JH1 campus in Johor, Malaysia. Proceeds will be used to finance the continued development and expansion of the campus.

Structured under PDG’s Green Finance Framework, the financing will support the development of JH1 in accordance with green building standards.

“This financing reflects the confidence of our banking partners, several of whom have supported JH1 since its earliest phases, in PDG's execution capabilities and deep hyperscaler partnerships,” said Rangu Salgame, chairman and CEO and co-founder of PDG.

The financing is underwritten by six banks: Affin Bank, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC, Standard Chartered, and UOB.

Located in Sedenak Tech Park, JH1 is a 200MW campus designed to support high-density AI and cloud workloads. The first 52MW phase of the campus was completed last year in July 2025. The company topped out the third building in late 2025.

PDG was founded in 2017 and has data centers in operation or development across China, Singapore, India, South Korea, Malaysia, and Japan. The company says its portfolio totals 1.8GW.

Private equity firm Warburg Pincus is PDG’s largest shareholder. The company is also backed by the Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, the UAE’s Mubadala, and Stonepeak.

The new financing builds on previous financing secured for earlier phases of the JH1 campus, which was first secured from three banks in April 2024, and subsequently upsized with four banks in October 2025.

stories.title: Nvidia chips pile up in Hong Kong as China withholds import approval
stories.summary: Large quantities of Nvidia chips have accumulated in Hong Kong warehouses as Chinese authorities deliberately withhold import approvals for advanced semiconductors. The stockpile illustrates Beijing's strategic calculation to reduce technological dependence on American suppliers despite domestic AI industry demand.
stories.why_it_matters: Hong Kong's role as a semiconductor transshipment hub is being compromised by geopolitical maneuvering, affecting logistics providers and distributors dependent on just-in-time delivery models. For Chinese AI companies, the withheld chips create project delays and force reliance on inferior domestic alternatives, while Nvidia loses revenue from one of its most significant historical markets.
stories.title_zh: NVIDIA芯片在香港堆积，因中国暂停进口审批
stories.summary_zh: 大量 Nvidia 芯片已在香港仓库中堆积，因为中国当局故意拖延先进半导体的进口审批。这种库存积压表明，尽管国内 AI 行业有需求，但北京方面战略性地考虑减少对美国供应商的技术依赖。
stories.why_zh: 香港作为半导体转运枢纽的角色正因地缘政治博弈而受损，影响依赖 just-in-time 交付模式的物流提供商和分销商。对于中国 AI 公司而言，被扣留的芯片造成项目延迟，并迫使其依赖较差的国内替代品，而 Nvidia 则失去了其历史上最重要的市场之一的收入。
stories.content:
The size of the stockpile reflects Beijing’s reluctance to increase reliance on US technology

ABOUT 600,000 of Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips are stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to mainland China, two people familiar with the matter said, as Beijing withholds approval for large-scale imports despite demand from technology firms.

The size of the stockpile of H200 chips, which has not previously been reported, reflects Beijing’s reluctance to increase reliance on US technology.

At the same time, Chinese companies need Nvidia’s advanced computing power to meet surging AI demand in the world’s second-largest economy.

China has allowed some of the chips to enter the country in recent months, three people familiar with the matter said. Several major Chinese internet companies have each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips in the past few months, one of the people said.

Three people said small quantities of chips had been shipped via intermediaries and indirect routes without specifying how many.

But Beijing has yet to approve large-volume imports into mainland China, the people said.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the National Development and Reform Commission did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Nvidia or Chinese tech companies Alibaba, ByteDance, DeepSeek and Tencent .

## H200 is not the most advanced, but very useful

The H200 is not Nvidia’s newest AI processor, but it has capabilities that Chinese alternatives have yet to match, making it useful for training AI models particularly when combined with Nvidia’s software.

US export controls since 2022 have sought to restrict China’s access to advanced Nvidia chips and the equipment needed to make them.

With authorised supply constrained, Chinese buyers have turned to intermediaries and indirect routes, pushing up prices in the unofficial market.

An eight-card H200 server was offered for more than six million yuan (US$900,000) in mainland China by the end of October, about three times its price a year earlier, one person familiar with the matter said.

Servers using Nvidia’s newer Blackwell chips, which fall under US export controls, were offered for more than 20 million yuan apiece, the person added.

## Tension over trade and technology

The H200 chip is caught in tension over trade and technology more broadly between Washington and Beijing.

The US barred exports of the H200 to China before US President Donald Trump’s administration gave Nvidia permission in 2025 to sell the chips to approved Chinese customers. The policy shift followed US-China trade negotiations.

Beijing has imposed its own constraints on H200 imports, reflecting concerns about dependence on US technology.

Technology publication The Information reported in July that Chinese officials had told companies, including Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek that they could receive permission to buy limited quantities of H200 chips for training AI models.

It reported that total approvals could amount to fewer than 200,000 chips and that Beijing wanted firms to prioritise Chinese processors for inference – the task of running AI models.

Reuters reported in October that ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent had ordered more than three million Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards, a less powerful export-compliant product, with a combined sticker price exceeding US$35 billion. REUTERS

stories.title: Universities must produce higher-skilled, tech-ready graduates — Anwar
stories.summary: Malaysian universities must urgently equip graduates with specialised skills in emerging technologies to meet the demands of global technology giants, including Google, which has announced plans to invest US$15 billion (RM60.96 billion) in the country.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: 大学必须培养更高技能、技术就绪的毕业生——安瓦尔
stories.content:
MELAKA (Nov 5): Malaysian universities must urgently equip graduates with specialised skills in emerging technologies to meet the demands of global technology giants, including Google, which has announced plans to invest US$15 billion (RM60.96 billion) in the country.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Alphabet and Google president and chief investment officer Ruth Porat had praised the capabilities, discipline and work ethic of Malaysian graduates but stressed the need for greater specialisation in certain fields.

He said higher education institutions must strengthen training in rapidly advancing technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing, to ensure graduates could capitalise on new employment opportunities and secure better wages.

“We must place greater emphasis on skills and expertise because without technology and technical capabilities, Malaysia cannot become a developed nation. Many new fields are emerging rapidly.

“Universities must therefore continue providing training to meet industry needs. Ultimately, we want our young people to earn significantly better wages and gain exposure to cutting-edge technologies that can help position Malaysia among the region’s most advanced nations,” he said at the Prime Minister's Golden Hand Awards 2026 ceremony at Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka (UTeM) here on Thursday.

Also present were Works Minister Datuk Seri Alexander Nanta Linggi, Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R Ramanan, Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir and Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek.

On Wednesday, Google announced plans to invest US$15 billion in Malaysia between 2027 and 2028 to expand its digital infrastructure, including developing data centre campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, to meet growing demand for AI and cloud computing services.

Elaborating, Anwar, who is also finance minister, said he had asked Porat about the skills required to support the company's investment.

“I asked her what was needed following the investment. She praised the achievements, discipline and knowledge of our young people, saying they were hardworking and qualified, but stressed the need for additional expertise in specific fields.

“University and college leaders must respond immediately to ensure our graduates are not only adequately trained to meet industry requirements but also continuously upgrade their skills,” he said.

Anwar said Porat had also cited Malaysia's political stability and clear government policies as key factors behind Google’s investment decision.

“I asked her to speak frankly about our strengths and weaknesses. She said Malaysia was stable, with no riots or frequent changes of government as in the past, and that this gave investors confidence,” he said.
